title: “Pélog”: Indonesian Gamelan in Prelude and Fugue No.5, Book II
content_blocks: On July 17 I wrote about Indonesian gamelan (see “Slendro”), and mentioned that different gamelan ensembles will be tuned to different scales. Where Slendro has five tones that are spread almost evenly across the octave, Pélog has seven tones, more similar to a Western scale, albeit with as many as three half-steps and one minor third. It thus has a very different feel from Slendro, and used for different purposes. Typically only five of those seven notes are used at any given moment, depending upon the modal “restraint”—a translation of the Indonesian word pathet—being used.

The prelude here serves as a “solo” instrumental introduction to the Pélog (pathet lima) tuning, with occasional percussive punctuations: a warm-up prior to the full ensemble accompanying an elaborate dance or parade ritual.  In the fugue we hear the stratified music of different pairs of instruments in a full gamelan ensemble, with higher instruments playing faster figurations and lower instruments playing slower forms of the same melody.  The fugal character of “chasing” or “fleeing” comes in how the main melody can be heard in multiple different layers.

Mika Sasaki brings out perfectly the ceremonial nature of the solemn introductory Prelude and the dance-like Fugue—including the difficult, repeated notes in the Fugue—in this combined video. Listen, too, to the percussion “break” in the middle of the fugue!
